# Results (generated by ml/write_results_md.py from results/*.json — do not edit by hand)

Every limit or simplification below ends with its next step: what, who, the metric that decides it, and when.

## 1. What the phone runs
- Frozen MobileNetV3-Large image backbone (ImageNet weights, Apache-2.0): **16.8 MB** ONNX, ~4 ms per photo on a laptop CPU. Phone speed is not yet measured. **Next step:** time the app on a low-cost Android phone and on an iPhone. Who: the team. Metric: median seconds from photo to answer, and first-load time. When: before the pilot starts.
- Shipped head **v3-2026-10-03-lab+field+other** (trained on lab + field photos, with an "other" answer for problems outside the five classes): **82 KB** JSON. Familiarity reference: **1400** stored training photos as int8 vectors (1000 lab, 400 field), **1798 KB**.
- The "other" answer is never shown as a diagnosis. When it is the top class, the app sends the photo to the officer ("looks like a different problem"), says the usual "not sure" sentence, and never counts the photo as rust.
- The ONNX path reproduces the Python pipeline: 25/25 same class on field photos, max embedding difference 0.0001; same decision on 7/7 demo samples; on Ugandan photos the embeddings differ by at most 4e-05.
- One backbone serves every head: the embedding standardisation baked into the ONNX file is computed on the lab training photos and kept for the shipped head, so the lab-only files (new-region simulation, starter kit) run on the same backbone.

## 2. Data
- **Lab photos** (7045 for training): 1,500 sampled per class from JMuBEN/JMuBEN2 (Kenya, Kirinyaga, arabica; many are rotated/flipped copies) plus half of the BRACOL photos we could recover (Brazil, arabica; 1,342 usable of 1,747). The other half of BRACOL (672 photos) is the lab calibration set, and lab accuracy is reported on it. JMuBEN's own validation split holds rotated or flipped copies of training leaves, so its score (100%) is not used.
- **Field photos**: RoCoLe (Ecuador, robusta, leaves on the plant, smartphone), 1385 healthy/rust photos labelled by the dataset authors, plus 167 red-spider-mite photos.
  - The shipped model trains on **1303** healthy/rust photos (751 healthy, 552 rust) and **154** mite photos as "other".
  - Never trained on: the 60 picture-card photos, the 7 demo samples (one is a mite photo), 16 healthy/rust photos that are identical or near-identical copies of a held-out photo, and every photo in the 12 copy groups that carry two different labels (12 mite photos and their rust or healthy copies). RoCoLe holds 71 pairs of identical or near-identical images (12 pairs carry two different labels, mostly mite vs rust); copies are always kept on the same side of every split.
- **Ugandan farm photos (external test; never used for training; one setting of the familiarity rule, `ood.local_nearest_cutoff`, was chosen on 40% of the copy clusters and is scored on the other part, section 3.3)**: "A Machine Learning Dataset for Classification of Common Coffee Leaf Diseases in Uganda" (Soroti University (Uganda), Mendeley Data, doi 10.17632/k36wnd6knb.1, CC BY 4.0). Close-ups of leaves on the plant, 256 × 256 px, labelled healthy, rust or Phoma by folder.
  - Of 3,322 listed files, 102 were empty. 28 photos have a near-identical copy in another class folder (rust vs Phoma), so their label is unknown and they are dropped. That leaves **3,192** photos (1,079 healthy, 1,016 rust, 1,097 Phoma).
  - The dataset mixes in rotated, flipped and brightened copies (1,411 files are byte-identical copies of another file). We group copies by image similarity into **1,351** distinct leaves (562 healthy, 476 rust, 313 Phoma; 934 are single photos, the largest group has 80). Each group counts once in every Ugandan number.
- **Lab-only model**: the same lab photos, no field photos. It gives the motivating finding (section 3.6), simulates a model meeting a new region's photo style, and is the starter-kit base.
- **Head v2** (the previous shipped head: lab + field photos, five classes, no "other") is kept for comparison; it is scored on the same folds and photos.

## 3. Findings

### 3.1 The shipped model on field photos (5-fold cross-validation)
Trained on lab photos plus field photos, the shipped model answers **91%** of healthy and rust field photos it has not seen and is right on **89%** of those answers. It names rust on **72%** of rust leaves and calls **6%** of healthy leaves a problem. Its confidence matches its accuracy (calibration error 0.04; 0 = perfect). Lab-style photos still work: 84% right on held-out BRACOL photos (84% for the lab-only model).

Compared with head v2 on the same folds, the "other" answer changes rust leaves named rust by **−3.6 points** (lower in 5 of 5 folds); 2.2% of rust leaves now go to the officer as "other" instead of being counted. The other three measures move by 1.1 points or less. What it buys is in section 3.2: far fewer mite photos counted as rust.

| Field photos (healthy + rust), never trained on | Shipped (head v3), mean of 5 folds | Spread (sd, points) | Head v2, same folds | v3 minus v2 (points) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answered (not "not sure") | 91% | 0.8 | 93% | −1.1 |
| Answers that are correct | 89% | 2.5 | 89% | −0.1 |
| Rust leaves named rust (of all rust leaves) | 72% | 4.1 | 76% | −3.6 |
| Healthy leaves called a problem (of all healthy leaves) | 6% | 3.1 | 6% | −0.1 |
| Rust leaves sent to the officer as "other" | 2.2% | 2.3 | 0% (no "other") | |
| Correct if forced to name one of the five classes | 87% | 2.8 | | |
| Calibration error (ECE) | 0.04 | 0.03 | | |

Second check on photos kept out from the start (the 60 picture-card photos, section 3.4): it answers 50 of 60, 88% of them correctly (head v2: 50 of 60, 90%). On the app's demo samples it answers 5 of the 6 healthy/rust photos correctly and says "not sure" to 1.

How it was measured: each fold's head was trained on all lab photos plus the other four folds (healthy, rust and mite photos; copy groups stay in one fold); its familiarity reference held only those folds' healthy and rust photos; its temperature, confidence threshold, familiarity cutoff and "other" constant were chosen on the BRACOL calibration half plus the other folds' out-of-fold predictions, so nothing was tuned on the photos it was scored on. The shipped head uses all training photos, with those values chosen the same way on all out-of-fold predictions (threshold 0.53, cutoff 0.494, temperature 1.43). Head v2 used the same folds and the same healthy/rust photos.

### 3.2 "Not sure" and "other problem" routing
The app answers only when three checks pass: the model is confident, the photo looks like the stored training photos, and the top class is not "other". Every other photo goes to the officer's review queue and stays out of the rust count until the officer labels it.

- **It sets aside the photos it would get wrong.** On the 9% of healthy and rust field photos the shipped model sends to the officer, it would have been right only 63% of the time if forced to answer, against 89% on the photos it answers. Reasons: low confidence (5.6% of photos), unfamiliar look (1.8%) and "looks like a different problem" (1.1%).
- **It protects the count when the photo style is new.** On farm photos from Uganda (section 3.3), the shipped model would be right on only 43% if forced to answer; the app sends 93% of them to the officer instead, almost all because they look unfamiliar (93% of all photos). In the new-region simulation (section 3.6), confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.29, worse than a coin flip), while comparing each photo with the stored training photos separates the new style almost perfectly (AUROC 0.999).

#### Problems outside the five classes: the "other" answer
**What head v3 adds.** Head v2 had five answers, so a photo of a pest it was never taught got one of them: it called 121 of the 167 red-spider-mite photos rust, which would inflate a village's rust count. Head v3 learns a sixth answer, "other", from 154 mite photos. The app never shows "other" as a diagnosis: the photo goes to the officer with the reason "looks like a different problem", and it never counts as rust.

Each mite photo below is scored by a head that never saw it or a copy of it (out-of-fold for the 154 photos used in training, the final head for the 13 never trained on):

| 167 mite photos | Shipped (head v3) | Head v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Sent to the officer (any reason) | **38%** | 14% |
| of which because "other" is the top class | 21% | — |
| Answered "rust" (counted as rust) | **85** | 121 |
| Answered "healthy" | 19 | 22 |
| Cross-validated, same mite photos and folds: sent to the officer | 39% (sd 7.4) | 9% (sd 3.8) |
| Cross-validated, same mite photos and folds: answered "rust" | 50% (sd 6.7) | 74% (sd 3.9) |

What it means for a rust count: across all RoCoLe field photos in the dataset's own mix (healthy, rust and mite), mite photos make up 15% of the "rust" answers with head v3, against 20% with head v2 (cross-validated). The "other" score separates mite photos from healthy and rust field photos with AUROC 0.84; the familiarity distance does so with 0.74 and confidence with 0.68. The familiarity reference is the same 1400 stored photos as head v2 (no mite photos), so the "unfamiliar" rule works as before; only the "other" score is new.

**What it costs, and the setting we ship.** Mite and rust look alike in these photos (12 copy groups even carry both labels). Trained as is, "other" takes many rust photos. Two choices beyond the v2 setup keep that in check: (1) the confidence threshold uses the same 90% rule as v2, checked on healthy, rust and lab photos; (2) a constant is added to the "other" score so that 1% of healthy and rust field photos (out-of-fold, chosen without the scored fold) have "other" as top class. Each setting below is cross-validated the same way:

| Setting | Rust leaves named rust | Healthy + rust photos answered | Mite photos sent to the officer | Mite photos answered "rust" (of 167) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Head v2 (no "other") | 76% | 93% | 14% | 121 |
| Head v3, "other" as trained, mite photos inside the threshold rule | 49% | 72% | 75% | 28 |
| Head v3, threshold rule as v2, no "other" constant | 55% | 80% | 71% | 33 |
| Head v3, threshold rule as v2, "other" constant at 0.5% | 74% | 93% | 29% | 96 |
| **Head v3, threshold rule as v2, "other" constant at 1% (shipped)** | 72% | 91% | 38% | 85 |
| Head v3, threshold rule as v2, "other" constant at 2% | 70% | 90% | 41% | 79 |
| Head v3, threshold rule as v2, "other" constant at 5% | 66% | 87% | 51% | 64 |

We ship the 1% setting: it names rust on 72% of rust leaves (−3.6 points against head v2, lower in 5 of 5 folds) and cuts mite photos counted as rust from 121 to 85. The 2.2% of rust leaves sent to the officer as "other" are not lost: they wait in the officer's queue and count once labelled. If the team prefers a smaller drop in rust named, the 0.5% setting gives 74% rust named and 96 mite photos counted as rust. The setting was picked after seeing this table, so the head v3 numbers carry a small selection effect. **Next step:** fix the "other" setting before the Kenyan test set is opened, then report on that set. Who: ML lead. Metric: rust leaves named rust and mite-like photos sent to the officer, on the Kenyan test set. When: before the Kenyan test set is opened (first pilot month).

What "other" does not fix yet (mite photos still counted as rust; one pest from one dataset; officer labels of only healthy and rust photos wear the "other" answer down) is in section 3.8, with the next step for each. The 38% of mite photos sent to the officer holds before any officer labels.

### 3.3 External test on Ugandan farm photos, and the officer learning loop there
The closest test we have to a new region: 3,192 photos of healthy, rust and Phoma leaves from farms in Uganda (1,351 distinct leaves after grouping copies; section 2). No Ugandan photo was used for training. One setting, the second familiarity check's cutoff, was chosen on 40% of the copy clusters; its clean numbers below come from the other part only. Each group of copies counts once.

**Without officer labels (the app as shipped).**

| Ugandan photos, never trained on | Shipped model (head v3) | 95% interval | Lab-only model |
|---|---|---|---|
| Photos answered (the rest go to the officer) | 7% | 5–8% | 8% |
| Answers that are correct | 52% | 41–62% | 56% |
| Right if forced to answer every photo | 43% | | 34% |
| Sent to the officer because the photo looks unfamiliar | 93% | | 92% |
| Rust leaves named rust (of all rust leaves) | 4% | 2–5% | 6% |
| Phoma leaves named Phoma (of all Phoma leaves) | 6% | 3–9% | 7% |
| Phoma leaves answered "rust" (of all Phoma leaves) | 9% | | 10% |
| Healthy leaves called a problem (of all healthy leaves) | 3% | 1–4% | 2% |

The 95% intervals come from resampling copy groups. What it means: the "not sure" check does its job in a new country. Forced to answer, the shipped model would be right on only 43% of Ugandan photos; the app instead sends 93% of them to the officer, mostly because they look unlike any stored photo, and calls only 3% of healthy leaves a problem. When forced, it calls 73% of rust leaves rust but only 27% of Phoma leaves Phoma (53% of Phoma leaves would be called rust), so Phoma is the look-alike most likely to reach a rust count here. **Next step:** train a head on half of the Ugandan copy groups (Phoma field photos included) and test it on the other half. Who: ML lead. Metric: Phoma leaves answered "rust" and rust leaves named rust, on the held-out half. When: before the pilot starts.

**With officer labels, the tool learns the new country and starts answering.** On the part of the Ugandan photos never used to choose any setting (805 copy groups), with the app's familiarity rule:

| Officer labels | Photos answered | Answers correct | Rust leaves named rust | Phoma leaves named Phoma | Healthy leaves called a problem | Previous rule: answered (correct) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **7%** | **53%** | 5% | 5% | 3.5% | 7% (53%) |
| 10 | **14%** | **80%** | 13% | 11% | 2.9% | 7% (65%) |
| 20 | **19%** | **85%** | 17% | 15% | 2.1% | 8% (72%) |
| 50 | **32%** | **92%** | 28% | 25% | 1.3% | 8% (85%) |
| 100 | **46%** | **94%** | 44% | 40% | 1.6% | 10% (91%) |

"Named" counts only answered photos; a photo sent to the officer counts as not named. Mean of 5 random pool/scored splits and label orders; the dataset's folder labels stand in for the officer.

- **What it means.** After 50 officer labels the tool answers 32% of Ugandan photos and is right on 92% of them; after 100, it answers 46% (94% correct), so the officer labels fewer photos by hand as the tool learns. The photos the new rule adds are right 94% of the time after 50 labels and 95% after 100. With no labels the two rules are the same (7% answered, 53% correct).
- **The rule.** A photo counts as familiar when its 10 nearest stored photos (shipped + officer-labelled) are close, as before, OR when its single nearest officer-labelled photo is within 0.494 (`ood.local_nearest_cutoff` in `model/head.json`; 1.0 × the shipped cutoff). The shipped stored photos never count for the second part, and with no officer labels the app behaves exactly as before. Threshold, temperature, the "other" route and the on-phone refit are unchanged. The previous rule needed 10 close stored photos, which the varied Ugandan photos rarely have: if every other Ugandan photo were stored, 81% would count as familiar.
- **How the setting was chosen (written down before the first run).** The Ugandan coarse copy clusters were split at random: 40% for choosing (546 copy groups) and the rest for testing (805). Candidates were 0.2 to 1.0 × the shipped cutoff; the rule was the largest value for which the photos the new rule adds are at least 85% correct at 10, 20, 50 and 100 labels. Every candidate passed; the chosen one's added photos were 96–97% correct. 1.0 × cutoff is the top of the candidate list; larger values were not tested.
- **Checks on other photos (pass/fail gates set in advance).** Ecuador new-region simulation: answers correct 74% / 75% / 82% → 75% / 76% / 82% at 10 / 20 / 50 labels (gate: no drop over 3 points), answered 61% / 82% / 91% → 85% / 89% / 93%. Mite photos with the shipped model: the share sent to the officer drops by 0.2, 1.4 and 1.7 points at 10, 50 and 100 labels (gate: at most 5); with head v2, which never trained on mite photos, 0.4, 1.9 and 2.0 points (reported, not a gate). The 60 picture-card photos: decisions identical (50 of 60 answered under both rules).
- **What it costs.** Healthy leaves called a problem rise from 0.8% to 1.3% after 50 labels and from 0.7% to 1.6% after 100: roughly double, still under 2%. With few labels the officer still sees most photos (14% answered after 10 labels). With a stricter grouping of near-copies, 40% are answered after 100 labels, 92% correctly. **Next step:** report photos answered and answers correct on the first 200 officer-labelled Kenyan pilot photos (the sealed Kenyan test set), with the app rule and the previous rule side by side. Who: ML lead. Metric: photos answered and answers correct after 50 and 100 labels; healthy leaves called a problem (must stay under 2%). When: first pilot month.
- **The head itself learns too.** On all Ugandan photos (both parts; same refit and rule), right if forced rises from 43% to 68% after 10 labels, 81% after 50 and 85% after 100 (coarser grouping: 82% after 100). The all-photo numbers with the app rule (33% answered, 90% correct after 50 labels; 47% and 93% after 100; 63% answered after 200) include the clusters used to choose the cutoff; the table above does not. Starting from the lab-only model: 34% answered after 50 labels and 48% after 100. The earlier figure of 9% answered after 100 labels (81% correct) is the previous rule on all photos.

Figure: `results/figs/uganda_learning_loop.png`. The limits of this test (Uganda, not Kenya; photo style; species; copies; folder labels; settings not tuned for Uganda) are in section 3.8, each with its next step.

### 3.4 People with a picture card vs the shipped AI (one-evening test)
Two team members, with no coffee training, labelled the same 60 field photos using only a picture card (two pictures and one line per problem), on a phone or laptop. The shipped AI was scored on the same photos with the same rule as the app. It was never trained on these photos.

| Who | Photos answered (not "not sure") | Answers correct | Healthy vs problem correct (of answered) | Correct out of all 60 | Median seconds per photo |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Team member A (picture card) | 97% | 59% | 91% | 57% | 2.4 |
| Team member B (picture card) | 100% | 57% | 97% | 57% | 2.3 |
| **AI as shipped** (head v3: lab + field photos + "other") | 83% | 88% | 88% | 73% | — |
| Reference: head v2 (lab + field photos, five classes) | 83% | 90% | 90% | 75% | — |
| Context: lab-only AI, no field labels (new-region simulation) | 0% | — | — | 0% | — |
| Context: lab-only AI after 50 officer-style field labels | 90% | 87% | 87% | 78% | — |

Right answer by true class, out of all photos of that class ("not sure" counts as not right):

| Who | Healthy (30) | Rust level 1 (17) | Rust level 2 (8) | Rust level 3 (3) | Rust level 4 (2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Team member A | 90% | 29% | 25% | 0% | 0% |
| Team member B | 97% | 18% | 12% | 0% | 50% |
| AI as shipped | 83% | 59% | 88% | 33% | 50% |
| Reference: head v2 | 83% | 59% | 88% | 67% | 50% |
| Context: lab-only AI after 50 labels | 77% | 88% | 88% | 33% | 50% |

What it means: with only the card, both people told sick leaves from healthy ones well (91%–97% of answers) but named rust on only 5–7 of the 30 rust photos; they often chose "brown eye spot" (13–19 times each). The shipped AI named rust on **19 of 30** (head v2: 20), called 4 of 30 healthy leaves a problem, and sent 17% of photos to the officer instead of guessing. The two people gave the same answer on 60% of photos. A card is enough to notice that something is wrong; the AI adds a consistent rust label, which is what a village rust count needs.

How "right" is decided: every RoCoLe photo carries the dataset authors' label (healthy, or rust at level 1 to 4). "Named rust" means the answer "rust" on a photo the authors labelled rust; the five answer options were the same for people and AI (healthy, rust, leaf miner, brown eye spot, Phoma, plus "not sure"). The AI's "other" answer counts as "not sure" here, because the app shows it that way. People saw copies resized to 900 px and the AI used the originals; on the resized copies the shipped AI makes the same decision on 59 of 60 photos.

What this test is and is not:
- Two team members (not farmers or plant experts, standing in for relay farmers) labelled 60 photos from one dataset (RoCoLe: Ecuador, robusta, on-plant; 30 healthy and 30 rust at levels 1 to 4: 17, 8, 3, 2 photos) in one evening. Relay farmers trained by the cooperative may do better. **Next step:** repeat the card test with relay farmers trained by the cooperative, on 60 officer-labelled Kenyan pilot photos. Who: the team with the cooperative. Metric: rust photos named rust and healthy-vs-problem correct, next to the AI on the same photos. When: first pilot month.
- The shipped AI has seen field photos of healthy, rust and red-spider-mite leaves from this dataset (never these 60); the people saw only lab-style pictures on the card. **Next step:** add field photos of each problem to the picture card before that test. Who: the team. Metric: rust photos named rust by people using the new card. When: before the relay-farmer card test.
- The lab-only rows are context from the new-region simulation; one of the 60 photos is an identical copy of a photo in its 50-label update. **Next step:** rebuild the 50-label demo update without that photo. Who: ML lead. Metric: the lab-only "after 50 labels" row on the 60 photos. When: after the challenge.

### 3.5 Village ranking (simulation at the shipped model's error rates)
Synthetic villages; the classifier's error rates are the shipped model's cross-validated rates (answers 91% of photos; calls 82% of answered rust photos rust and 6% of answered healthy photos rust). It ranks rust already seen; it does not predict outbreaks. Across 40 villages per round with about 6.6 real outbreaks (rust share above 25%):

| Rule | False alarms per round | Missed outbreaks per round | Real outbreaks among the 5 villages visited first |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw share of rust photos | 3.4 | 1.6 | 3.5 |
| Small-sample adjusted (the app's rule: alert when P(share > 25%) > 0.5) | 1.0 | 3.0 | 3.7 |

The adjustment cuts false alarms (3.4 → 1.0) and sends the officer to more real outbreaks first (3.5 → 3.7 of 5). It misses more villages that sit near the 25% line (1.6 → 3.0); those villages still appear in the ranked list, just below the alert line. At head v2's error rates the same comparison gives 3.6 → 1.1 false alarms and 1.5 → 2.9 misses; with the lab-only model after 50 labels (a less accurate operating point), 8.4 → 5.3 false alarms and 1.2 → 1.9 misses. The villages are synthetic and hold only healthy and rust leaves, so this table does not show the main gain of the "other" answer (fewer mite photos counted as rust, section 3.2). **Next step:** replay both alert rules on pilot visit data and re-set the alert line. Who: ML lead with the cooperative extension officer. Metric: false alarms and missed outbreaks against the officer's own village checks. When: after the first 3 months of pilot visits.

### 3.6 Why the shipped model trains on field photos (the lab-only result)
This is the finding that shaped the design. Trained on lab photos only, the head is right 84% of the time on held-out lab photos but only **2.5%** on field photos if forced to answer, while reporting **93%** average confidence (it calls almost every field leaf Phoma). Its confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.29); comparing each photo with the stored training photos does (AUROC 0.999), and the app says "not sure" to 99.6% of those field photos instead of guessing.

Three design choices follow from it:
- **Train on photos taken the way relay farmers will take them.** Adding field photos to training lifts forced field accuracy to 87% (cross-validated), and lab accuracy stays at 84%.
- **Keep the familiarity check for photo styles the model has not seen.** It did the same job on the Ugandan photos (section 3.3).
- **Let the officer's labels adapt the model.** We simulate a new region by starting from the lab-only model and treating the field photos as the new region's photos. When the officer labels photos, the head is refit on the phone (pulled toward the starting model) and the labelled photos join the familiarity reference:

| Officer labels | Photos answered | Answers correct | Answers correct, local labels only (no starting model) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| 10 | 85% | 75% | 67% |
| 20 | 89% | 76% | 70% |
| 50 | 93% | 82% | 81% |
| 100 | 96% | 85% | 84% |
| 200 | 97% | 86% | 85% |

After 50 labels the tool answers 93% of the new region's photos, 82% correctly. A starting model matters most when labels are few (75% vs 67% correct at 10 labels). An update to share with other phones is ~13 KB for the head plus 1284 bytes per labelled photo. These numbers use the app's familiarity rule, including the nearest-officer-photo check; with the previous rule (10 nearest stored photos only) the tool answered 61% after 10 labels and 91% after 50 (82% correct). On the more varied Ugandan photos the check opens more slowly (section 3.3).

### 3.7 Size vs accuracy
In the new-region setting (lab-only training, no field labels), a 5x larger backbone (DINOv2-small, 21.6M parameters, ~87 MB) is right 49% of the time on field photos (vs 2.5% for MobileNetV3); after 50 labels it answers 58% of photos with 90% correct. Training the small backbone on field photos does better than that (87% forced accuracy, cross-validated), so we ship the 16.8 MB backbone that fits the side-loading constraint. A larger backbone remains an option where phones allow it.

### 3.8 Remaining limits and the next step for each
**Where the evidence comes from**
- **No Kenyan farm photos yet.** Field training photos are Ecuadorian robusta (RoCoLe); the external test is from Uganda (healthy, rust, Phoma). None comes from Kenyan farms, where the tool would be used. **Next step:** keep the first 200 officer-labelled Kenyan pilot photos aside as a Kenyan test set, never trained on. Who: the team with the cooperative extension officer. Metric: photos answered, answers correct and rust leaves named rust. When: first pilot month.
- **No plant IDs in RoCoLe.** Leaves of one plant can sit in both a training and a test fold, so the cross-validated numbers may be optimistic. We keep identical and near-identical images on one side of every split, and the 60 picture-card photos give a second check. **Next step:** record plot and plant with every pilot photo, so tests can hold out whole farms. Who: the team adds the fields to the app; relay farmers fill them in. Metric: answers correct on held-out farms against randomly held-out photos. When: from the first pilot visit.
- **Labels come from the dataset authors.** RoCoLe's labels and the Ugandan folder labels stand in for an extension officer, in the cross-validation and in both learning loops. Some photos in the Ugandan Phoma folder show rust-like orange spots, so some label noise likely remains after dropping the 28 photos with a copy in another folder. **Next step:** the extension officer relabels 100 random RoCoLe photos and 100 random Ugandan photos. Who: cooperative extension officer. Metric: share of photos where the officer agrees with the dataset label. When: pilot week 1.
- **RoCoLe copy groups with two labels are dropped.** 12 groups of identical or near-identical RoCoLe images carry two labels (mostly mite and rust). They are out of training and out of the cross-validation; their 12 mite photos are scored only in the 167-photo count of section 3.2. **Next step:** the extension officer relabels the photos in these groups; groups with an agreed label go back into training. Who: extension officer. Metric: share of the 12 groups with an agreed label. When: pilot onboarding, week 1.
- **Copies in the Ugandan photos.** We group copies by image similarity; copies that were also cropped or strongly brightened can escape the grouping, so a few near-copies may sit in both the pool and the test half of the learning loop. The stricter grouping (section 3.3) shows how much this matters: on the Ugandan test part, 40% answered after 100 labels (92% correct) against 46% (94%). **Next step:** ask the dataset authors for the original file list (before copies were made) and rerun with exact groups. Who: the team, by email. Metric: photos answered and answers correct with exact groups against ours. When: after the challenge.
- **Ugandan photo style.** Close-ups of single leaves on the plant, outdoors in daylight, stored at 256 × 256 px; a check by eye of about 70 photos found a few with soil behind the leaf, so some may be fallen or held leaves. The phone sees full-size photos framed by a relay farmer. **Next step:** on the first 100 pilot photos, compare full-size photos with the same photos cut to 256 × 256 px. Who: the team. Metric: photos answered and answers correct, full-size against cut. When: pilot week 1.
- **Coffee species in the Ugandan photos is not stated** (Uganda grows robusta and arabica). **Next step:** record the coffee species at each plot visit and report results by species. Who: the extension officer at each plot visit. Metric: answers correct by species. When: from the first pilot visit.

**What the tool does in a new region**
- **With few officer labels, the officer still sees most photos in a new region.** On the Ugandan test part the app answers 14% of photos after 10 labels and 32% after 50 (Ecuador simulation: 93% after 50). The second familiarity check that opens it was chosen on Ugandan photos (a separate part) and checked on Ecuador and mite photos, not on Kenyan photos; it roughly doubles healthy leaves called a problem (0.7% → 1.6% after 100 labels). **Next step:** report photos answered and answers correct on the first 200 officer-labelled Kenyan pilot photos (the sealed Kenyan test set), with the app rule and the previous rule side by side. Who: ML lead. Metric: photos answered and answers correct after 50 and 100 labels; healthy leaves called a problem (must stay under 2%). When: first pilot month.
- **Phoma reaches the rust count in Uganda.** 9% of Ugandan Phoma leaves are answered "rust", against 6% named Phoma; if forced, 53% would be called rust. The shipped head has seen Phoma only in lab photos. **Next step:** train a head on half of the Ugandan copy groups (Phoma field photos included) and test it on the other half. Who: ML lead. Metric: Phoma leaves answered "rust" and rust leaves named rust, on the held-out half. When: before the pilot starts.
- **Settings not tuned for a new region.** The learning-step strength (how hard the on-phone update pulls toward the shipped head), the answer threshold and the familiarity cutoff are the shipped values; none was tuned on Ugandan or Kenyan photos. **Next step:** re-tune the learning-step strength, answer threshold and familiarity cutoff on the first pilot labels, using an inner split of the labelled photos only. Who: ML lead. Metric: photos answered and answers correct after 50 labels. When: after the first 50 pilot labels.

**Problems outside the five classes**
- **Mite photos still reach the rust count.** 85 of 167 mite photos are still answered "rust", and the demo's mite sample is answered "healthy". In the app now: 1 in 10 answered photos also goes to the officer as a spot check, the officer's "Different problem (not in list)" label trains the "other" class in the on-phone update, and the plot card never says a plot is disease-free. **Next step:** the extension officer labels every "Different problem" photo in the review queue, and the ML lead retrains "other" with them. Who: extension officer and ML lead. Metric: mite-like photos counted as rust (must fall) and rust leaves named rust (must stay within 3 points of head v3, cross-validated); the update is kept only if both hold. When: pilot week 4.
- **Officer labels of only healthy and rust photos wear down the "other" answer** (found by the mite test of the familiarity rule; not caused by that rule). With the shipped head and no labels, 71% of the 167 mite photos go to the officer (flattering: head v3 trained on 154 of them; the fair figure is 38%, section 3.2). After 10 officer labels of healthy and rust photos it is 27%, after 100 15%; most of the rest are answered "rust" (45% after 10 labels, 67% after 100). The cause is the head refit, not the added photos: refitting alone gives 27% / 17% / 16% after 10 / 50 / 100 labels; adding the photos without refitting stays at 71%. So the 38% figure holds only before any officer labels; the officer's spot check and "Different problem" labels remain the safeguard. **Next step:** keep the "other" weights fixed during the on-phone refit, or mix stored "other" rows into it, and rerun the mite test of ml/eval_familiarity_rule.py. Who: ML lead. Metric: mite photos sent to the officer after 10, 50 and 100 healthy/rust labels (target: within 5 points of the no-label level) with rust leaves named rust unchanged. When: before the pilot starts.
- **"Other" knows one pest from one dataset** (red spider mite, Ecuadorian robusta). Brown eye spot in the field, other pests and nutrient deficiency are not in it. Without "other", photos of an untaught problem are no longer caught once field photos are familiar: the lab-only model after 50 field labels says "not sure" to only 19% of mite photos. **Next step:** keep 1 in 5 officer-labelled "Different problem" photos out of training as a test set for the "other" answer. Who: ML lead. Metric: share of those photos sent to the officer (target: above head v3's 38% on mite photos). When: report at pilot week 4.
- **A few "Different problem" labels can swing the on-phone update** (found in a browser check on the 7 demo photos, 3 Oct; not part of this pipeline). An update built from one "Different problem" label and no healthy label sent the healthy demo photos to the officer as "looks like a different problem"; with one healthy and one rust label added, every demo photo came back as before. This errs toward the officer (more photos queued), not toward a wrong answer. **Next step:** test the on-phone update with 1–20 officer labels that include "Different problem", and add a rule (a stronger pull toward the shipped model for "other", or a minimum number of healthy and rust labels) if healthy photos go to "other". Who: ML lead. Metric: healthy field photos sent to "other" after the update (shipped model: 0.4%). When: before the pilot starts.
- **Two choices beyond the v2 setup, one picked after seeing results** (section 3.2): the threshold rule is checked on healthy, rust and lab photos only, and a constant on the "other" score sends 1% of healthy and rust photos to "other". The 1% value was picked after seeing the cross-validated trade-off, so the head v3 numbers carry a small selection effect. **Next step:** fix the "other" setting before the Kenyan test set is opened, then report on that set. Who: ML lead. Metric: rust leaves named rust and mite-like photos sent to the officer, on the Kenyan test set. When: before the Kenyan test set is opened (first pilot month).

**Simulations and small tests**
- **The village ranking is a simulation** with synthetic villages; only the classifier's error rates are measured. **Next step:** replay both alert rules on pilot visit data and re-set the alert line. Who: ML lead with the cooperative extension officer. Metric: false alarms and missed outbreaks against the officer's own village checks. When: after the first 3 months of pilot visits.
- **The picture-card test** used two team members for one evening, on 60 RoCoLe photos. **Next step:** repeat the card test with relay farmers trained by the cooperative, on 60 officer-labelled Kenyan pilot photos. Who: the team with the cooperative. Metric: rust photos named rust and healthy-vs-problem correct, next to the AI on the same photos. When: first pilot month.
- **Phone speed is not measured**; the ~4 ms per photo is on a laptop CPU. **Next step:** time the app on a low-cost Android phone and on an iPhone. Who: the team. Metric: median seconds from photo to answer, and first-load time. When: before the pilot starts.
